passage:
Thursday night

Two more days until the bank calls with the interview result. Tonight after Isha prayer I told Allah that if I get this job I will keep three extra fasts and give to the madrasa near Ammi's house. I said it out loud, like a deal.
Then I felt silly. Is that how it works? You pay in hunger and He pays in jobs?
Ammi saw my face at dinner. "Nazia beti, promising is not wrong. But He also gave you a brain. Did you prepare for the second round?"
I hadn't. I was so busy praying I forgot to practise the case questions.
So I opened my laptop and did two mock cases till midnight. I'll still keep the fasts either way, I think. Not as payment. More like saying thank you, or saying I'm still here even if the answer is no.

qa.q: What did the narrator promise to do if the bank job came through?
qa.a: Nazia promised to keep three extra fasts and give to the madrasa near Ammi's house.

qa.q: How did Nazia feel right after making her promise out loud, and why?
qa.a: She felt silly and uneasy, because the promise suddenly seemed like a trade where she pays in hunger and God pays in jobs.

qa.q: What small step helped Nazia hold her promise more lightly?
qa.a: She opened her laptop and practised two mock cases, so her hope rested on preparation as well as prayer.

qa.q: How might Ammi see Nazia's promise at dinner?
qa.a: Ammi seems gentle about it; she does not mock the promise, but she wants Nazia to remember that effort matters too.

grounding: A young adult bargains with God over a job result and learns to keep the promise as sincere devotion while still putting in honest effort.

passage:
Shalini: results out. cleared group 1, failed group 2 again 😢
Manjula: oh Shalu, my poor girl. I'm so sorry. Where are you?
Shalini: on the terrace. I walked up the hill temple barefoot in March, remember? I promised coconuts every Tuesday if I cleared both groups.
Shalini: so either God didn't want it or I don't deserve it.
Manjula: or the paper was brutal and you had flu the week before 🙁
Manjula: a no this time isn't a verdict on you.
Shalini: then what was the point of the walk?
Manjula: you tell me. how did you feel walking up?
Shalini: …calm. first calm day in months.
Manjula: maybe keep that part. and let's look at which chapters sank you. Saturday, my place?
Shalini: ok 🙏 bring the answer key

qa.q: Where was Shalini when she messaged Manjula about her results?
qa.a: Shalini was on the terrace.

qa.q: What does Shalini's message about not deserving it suggest she is feeling?
qa.a: She feels ashamed and crushed, as if failing group 2 proves God judged her unworthy after her barefoot walk and promise.

qa.q: What did Manjula do that helped, and why did it work?
qa.a: She gently separated the result from Shalini's worth and then offered a practical Saturday plan to study the weak chapters, so hope and effort both stayed alive.

qa.q: How does Manjula see the moment when Shalini asks what the walk was for?
qa.a: Manjula sees that the walk gave Shalini real calm, so she wants her to keep that faith without treating it as a failed payment.

grounding: After an exam bargain with God ends in a no, a friend helps the protagonist see that the result is not a judgement of her worth and that effort still matters.

passage:
Kitchen coordinator's note, Sunday langar

Payal came in at five again today, before the dal was even soaked, and stayed through the last round of washing. That is her third double shift this month. She moves fast, laughs with the aunties at the rotis, and quietly seats the construction workers from the site next door when they hesitate at the gate.
At the tea break I saw Vinita, from the committee, telling her that 'real sevadars' sponsor a full day's meal and get their family name read out. Payal's smile went stiff. She said she'd think about it.
Afterwards I sat with her on the steps. I told her the kitchen needs her hands more than her money, that nobody's name is read out for washing pots, and that she can say no. She let out a long breath and said she'd been lying awake over it.

qa.q: How many double shifts had Payal done that month?
qa.a: It was her third double shift that month.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling after Vinita spoke to her about sponsoring a meal?
qa.a: She felt pressured and uneasy; her smile went stiff, and later she admitted she had been lying awake over it.

qa.q: How did the coordinator support Payal, and why did it matter?
qa.a: They sat with her, told her the kitchen needs her hands more than her money, and made clear she could say no, which took away the pressure to give beyond what she could.

qa.q: How might the construction workers experience Payal seating them at the langar?
qa.a: They may feel welcome instead of unsure, because she noticed them hesitating at the gate and made space for them to eat like anyone else.

grounding: A young volunteer finds meaning in serving at a community kitchen, is pressured to give for status, and an adult reminds her that service need not go beyond her means.

passage:
Sunday. Late.

Annadanam day at the temple. I was on the rice counter from eleven, ladling onto banana leaves till my wrist ached. Best ache of the week, honestly.
Pooja aunty caught me at the tap. "Dhruv beta, you've been coming every Sunday for a year. We'll put your name on the donor board, near the entrance."
I said no thanks. I haven't donated anything; I just serve rice. She looked a bit hurt, like I'd refused a gift.
Then a man in a cap stood at the edge of the hall, not sure if he could sit. He asked me, quietly, "Anyone can eat here?" I said yes, and put a leaf down for him next to a group of college boys.
That moment beat any board. I want to keep it this way: I show up, I serve, nobody has to know my name.

qa.q: What was Dhruv doing at the temple from eleven?
qa.a: He was on the rice counter, ladling rice onto banana leaves.

qa.q: Why did Dhruv feel uncomfortable about having his name on the donor board?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and a little embarrassed, because he had only served rice, not donated, and he wanted his service to stay quiet rather than bring him status.

qa.q: What could Dhruv say to Pooja aunty next time so she does not feel brushed off?
qa.a: He could thank her warmly for noticing him and explain that serving without a name on the board is what gives him joy.

qa.q: How might the man in the cap see Dhruv's answer?
qa.a: He probably felt relieved and welcomed, since he was unsure he was allowed to eat until Dhruv said yes and set a leaf down for him.

grounding: A young man finds meaning in serving food at his temple, turns down public recognition, and makes sure a stranger feels the meal is open to all.

passage:
So, Pallavi, you asked why I went quiet in the car on Friday. Okay.
There was this man at the petrol pump near the flyover. Clean shirt, bag on his shoulder. 'Behenji,' he said, his wallet was stolen and he needed money for a bus to Nashik. And my whole body went stiff. My brother got taken by exactly that story last year, the same sad face, the same bus.
Part of me wanted to just drive off. Part of me thought, what if it's true?
So I did the middle thing. I said, 'I'm Nikita, I won't give cash, but I can buy you a meal from that stall, and there's a police booth right there if you need help getting home.'
He took the vada pav, didn't go to the booth. I still don't know if he was honest. I felt mean and sensible at the same time.

qa.q: What did the man at the petrol pump say he needed money for?
qa.a: 'Behenji,' he said, his wallet was stolen and he needed money for a bus to Nashik.

qa.q: What was Nikita feeling when the man asked for money?
qa.a: She felt afraid and torn, stiff with the memory of her brother being tricked, yet worried the man's story might be true.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Nikita, and why?
qa.a: Buying him a meal and pointing to the police booth let her help safely without handing over cash, so she respected her caution and still stayed kind.

qa.q: How might the man have seen Nikita's offer?
qa.a: If his story was true, he may have felt some relief at the food but frustrated not to get bus fare; if it was not, her offer quietly left him nothing to exploit.

grounding: A young woman hesitates when a stranger asks for money because she fears a scam, and chooses safe help that honours her instinct without making her hard-hearted.

passage:
Monday: Jyoti was locking her scooter outside the office at nine at night when a woman asked for a lift to the hospital. Jyoti said 'sorry, no' and rode off fast, heart pounding. She couldn't sleep, wondering if the woman had been in real trouble.
Wednesday: At lunch she told Chaitanya. He listened and said, 'You weren't wrong to be careful at night. But you could have called an auto or the helpline for her. That's still help.' Jyoti saved the city helpline and the nearest auto stand number in her phone.
Saturday: An old man outside the metro asked her for money for medicine. Her stomach tightened again. This time she walked him to the pharmacy counter and asked the chemist to help him, then showed him the station help desk. He blessed her twice. She went home steadier.

qa.q: What did Jyoti save in her phone on Wednesday?
qa.a: She saved the city helpline and the nearest auto stand number.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel after refusing the woman on Monday night?
qa.a: She felt guilty and restless; she could not sleep, wondering if the woman had been in real trouble.

qa.q: What changed in how Jyoti responded between Monday and Saturday?
qa.a: On Monday she only refused, but by Saturday she kept her caution and still helped safely by taking the man to the pharmacy counter and the station help desk.

qa.q: How might the old man outside the metro have seen Jyoti's help?
qa.a: He likely felt grateful and respected, since she did not wave him away but made sure someone could actually help him; he blessed her twice.

grounding: Over a week a young woman moves from fearful refusal to safe, practical help for strangers, trusting her caution without becoming hard-hearted.

passage:
The motorbike coughed twice and died on the kacha road past Sonpur, just as the sun dropped behind the sugarcane. Hemant kicked the starter until his leg shook. His phone showed one bar. Amma was waiting at home with her evening tablets on the shelf.
A woman came out from a tin-roofed tea shack with a lantern. "Chain or petrol?" she asked. Her name was Pallavi, and her brother fixed pumps in the next village. She called him, poured Hemant tea in a steel glass, and refused to take anything for it.
Her brother arrived on a cycle, tightened a loose plug wire in two minutes, and laughed at Hemant's thanks.
Hemant pressed his hands together. "Can I have your number? If you ever come to Barhaj, you eat at our house." She wrote it on the back of a matchbox.
On the ride home he stopped for a boy pushing a punctured cycle, and gave him a lift to the pump.

qa.q: What was wrong with Hemant's motorbike?
qa.a: A loose plug wire, which Pallavi's brother tightened in two minutes.

qa.q: How did Hemant feel when the bike died, and what shows it?
qa.a: He felt anxious and stranded; he kicked the starter until his leg shook, his phone had one bar, and Amma was waiting at home.

qa.q: How did Hemant show his gratitude well?
qa.a: He thanked them warmly, asked for Pallavi's number and invited her to eat at his house, and then passed the kindness on by helping a boy with a punctured cycle.

qa.q: How might Pallavi see helping a stranger at dusk?
qa.a: She seems to treat it as ordinary decency; she offers tea, refuses payment, and calls her brother as if helping is simply what neighbours on that road do.

grounding: A young man stranded at dusk is helped by a stranger, thanks her warmly, takes her number and passes the kindness on the same evening.

passage:
The car slid on black ice outside Tromsø and stopped nose-down in a snowbank. Rafael sat gripping the wheel, breath loud in his ears. The engine had cut out. His hands would not stop shaking.
Headlights. A pickup pulled over and a man in a red wool hat tapped on the glass. "You hurt? I'm Liam. Stay in the warm, I'll call it in."
Liam phoned the road service, handed Rafael a flask of coffee and a spare blanket, and stood by the car with a torch for forty minutes until the tow truck came.
When it was over, Rafael hugged him, which surprised them both. "I don't even know how to thank you."
"Next time you see someone in a ditch, stop," Liam said, and gave him his number.
In March Rafael pulled over for a family with a flat tyre, and texted Liam a photo.

qa.q: How long did Liam wait with Rafael before the tow truck came?
qa.a: He stood by the car with a torch for forty minutes.

qa.q: What was Rafael feeling just after the car slid, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He was frightened; he gripped the wheel, his breath was loud in his ears, and his hands would not stop shaking.

qa.q: What did Rafael do that turned his gratitude into something lasting?
qa.a: He thanked Liam warmly, kept his number, and months later stopped to help a family with a flat tyre, then texted Liam a photo.

qa.q: How might Liam feel when he gets Rafael's photo in March?
qa.a: He would likely feel touched and glad, seeing that his one cold evening of help was passed on to another family.

grounding: A stranger helps the protagonist after a car skids off an icy road, and the protagonist thanks him, stays in contact and passes the kindness on.
